coverageNote: Enumerated from disk: 11 units (10 sub-domain directories + the domain root), 64 files — exactly matching the expected 11/64. Every unit directory carries both an *-index.md and a *-cx.md; the domain root carries digital-goods-marketplace-index.md + digital-goods-marketplace-cx.md. The Children table's claim of '10 sub-domains, 42 leaf features' was verified against the filesystem: 4+6+5+4+4+3+5+5+3+3 = 42 leaf feature files. All 64 files were processed. Read in full: both domain-root files, all 10 sub-domain indexes and CX files, and every leaf feature's Overview / Behavior / Happy Path / Edge Cases / States / Decisions sections. Rationale-only sections (Deep Think Annotations, Cross-Cut Notes) were read as condensed extracts since they carry hypothesis-and-verdict reasoning rather than normative behaviour; their verdicts were cross-checked against the corresponding Decisions rows. In addition, exhaustive automated extraction was run across all 64 files for: every Open Questions row (206 rows — all carry both an owner and a deferral target, or are struck through as resolved), every [PENDING]/[OWNER]/[DEFERRED] tracking marker with context, every numeric threshold and duration, every occurrence of unresolved-state language, and every mention of self-purchase. Dimensions 4 (Constraint Explicitness) and 6 (Competitive Positioning) are marked N/A across all units: they are owned by meta/constraints.md and meta/competitive-landscape.md, which are outside this domain's scope. Dimension 5 is additionally N/A for 14.06 and 14.10, which make no quantified commitments. Overall this domain is of unusually high quality — numeric thresholds (72 h grant windows, 7-year waiver retention, 120-day/13-month chargeback windows, 30-day promo suppression, P95 < 300 ms audition) are consistent across every file that cites them, and open-question tracking is essentially perfect. Several apparent gaps were investigated and refuted: the vendor-exit x rent-to-own 'open gap' in the domain CX is properly tracked at 14.07.03 Q-02 ([OWNER] -> /create-prd); the 14.01 CX 'unresolved case' on seat-satisfied dependencies is resolved by 14.01.03 D-03; the 14.03 CX 'unresolved' in-flight revocation is resolved by 14.03.01 D-05 and domain CX-23; and the 14.09.01 D-08/D-15 'fires for every buyer' vs 'does not fire' tension resolves cleanly because D-08's scope is explicitly territorial.

findings.claim: Silent contradiction across four features on whether a vendor may buy their own product. 14.01.01 and 14.08.01 state self-purchase is BLOCKED with no buy control rendered; 14.02.01, 14.04.01 and 14.07.01 state it is PERMITTED and flagged at issuance, with 14.02.01 DT-10 asserting that personas.md positively forbids blocking it. Neither side carries a [PENDING]/[OWNER] marker, and each side cites the other's file as authority. The two readings produce different UI (buy control present or absent), different data (an entitlement minted and flagged, or no entitlement at all), and different downstream logic (14.10/14.07.05 self-purchase exclusion filters are dead code under the blocked reading).
findings.evidence: BLOCKED side — 14.01.01-digital-product-listing-spec-sheet.md:127 (Edge Cases): "| **Vendor tries to buy their own listing** | Blocked. Self-purchase is a free path to manufactured sales rank and a laundering surface, and it is the marketplace half of the Musician anti-persona (gaming reputation) | Vendor: no buy control. \"You're the vendor — use *View as buyer* to see this listing as a customer.\" |" · 14.01.01-digital-product-listing-spec-sheet.md:213 (D-09): "Self-purchase is blocked on the same surface (sales-rank gaming, laundering)." · 14.08.01-vendor-onboarding-product-submission.md:134 (Edge Case 13): "| 13 | **Vendor submits their own product and later buys it** | Blocked — self-purchase games sales rank and is a laundering surface (14.01.01 D-09). Their own placement mints a zero-price self-entitlement instead (14.02.05 D-16). | No buy control. \"You're the vendor — use *View as buyer*.\" |"  ||  PERMITTED side — 14.02.01-licence-issuance-entitlement-record.md:201 (D-11): "| D-11 | **Self-purchase is permitted and flagged** at issuance (holder principal == the product's vendor principal, or an org the vendor controls); downstream excludes it from payout, sales rank, reviews and loyalty accrual | Per DT-10. personas.md forbids blocking it — one human is vendor and buyer in the same day. Without the flag, wash-trading rank on a store with no reputation is free and undetectable. Evaluated per order line against the product's vendor, never against the cart. |" · 14.02.01-licence-issuance-entitlement-record.md:158 (DT-10): "A vendor buying their own product is therefore **normal** and cannot be blocked." · 14.02.01-licence-issuance-entitlement-record.md:105 (Edge Cases): "| **Vendor buys their own product** ... | Permitted (a producer legitimately buys a colleague's pack, and a vendor's own principal may hold an org's copy), but **flagged at issuance** as self-purchase" · 14.04.01-sample-loop-pack-catalog.md:174: "Purchase permitted; **excluded from download counts, rankings and pool accrual** by same-payee detection. Not blocked — blocking it teaches vendors to use a second account, which is worse." · 14.07.01-perpetual-purchase-ownership.md:140: "| **Vendor buys their own perpetual product** | Permitted and flagged (14.02.01 D-11)" · digital-goods-marketplace-cx.md:411 (CX-21): "3. **Permission intersection**: Self-purchase detection excludes a contributor buying their own pack from their earnings."
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent which rule governs: render a buy control for the vendor and mint a flagged entitlement, or suppress the control entirely. 14.08.01's proposed substitute (a zero-price self-entitlement per 14.02.05 D-16) additionally conflates *placing your own product into a project* with *purchasing it*, which D-16 does not cover, so the blocked reading leaves the vendor-buys-own-product path with no defined entitlement at all.

findings.claim: 23 tracking markers across 19 files defer to `/ideate-discover Step 5 deepening` — a pipeline stage that has already completed. Nothing downstream will ever pick these up, so the deferral target is dead and the tracking is malformed. The authors demonstrably know to re-point stale deferrals (they did exactly that for the index-level Open Questions rows, which read "Deferral re-pointed from the completed `/ideate-validate`"), but the fix was applied only to Open Questions tables and not to these in-body markers. 11 of the 23 sit on CX "Role scoping" or "State transition conflict" slots (documentation completeness); the other ~9 sit in Edge Cases tables where they are the entire resolution column for a named failure scenario, leaving real product behaviour undefined with no owner.

Findings #003, #005, #006, #007 and #008 are the specific behaviour-bearing instances.

findings.claim: 14.02.03's two sharpest failure modes — money captured while the third-party DRM deposit fails, and a bridged third-party account belonging to someone other than the buyer — have a dead deferral target and are covered by none of the file's three tracked Open Questions (Q-01 reseller status, Q-02 refundability of bridged products, Q-03 whether offline activation exists at all). The first leaves a buyer charged with no entitlement in either system; the second is an undeclared change of holder that bypasses the entire 14.06 transfer-policy apparatus.
findings.evidence: 14.02.03-offline-activation-drm-bridges.md:61 (Edge Cases): "| Third-party DRM provider is down at purchase | Payment taken, deposit fails | `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` — the payment/deposit atomicity problem, harder than 14.02.01's because the second system isn't ours |" · 14.02.03-offline-activation-drm-bridges.md:63: "| Third-party account linked to a different person than the buyer | Effectively an undeclared gift/transfer, bypassing 14.06 | `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` |" · The file's full tracked question set, 14.02.03-offline-activation-drm-bridges.md:101-103, covers only reseller status (Q-01), refundability (Q-02, resolved) and whether offline activation should exist (Q-03) — none reaches either row. Contrast 14.02.01-licence-issuance-entitlement-record.md:192 (D-02), which locks the in-house case hard: "Issuance is atomic with **order completion** — for a paid order, confirmed payment capture ... A payment without an entitlement, or vice versa, are both unacceptable failures with no clean recovery."
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent the compensating behaviour when capture succeeds and the third-party deposit fails — auto-void, auto-refund, retry with a queue, or mint a pending-payment-style placeholder — and must invent whether a mismatched third-party account is refused at deposit, permitted silently, or routed through 14.06's transfer policy.

findings.claim: 14.05.04's minimum tag density is both unquantified and self-contradictory as to whether it is advisory or enforced. D-03's own title says the platform 'recommends' a minimum 'rather than accepting any interval' — recommendation and refusal are opposite mechanisms. The Behavior section states the requirement only in untestable terms, the Happy Path leaves the interval entirely to the producer, and the States table gates publish on the *presence* of a tag but not on its density. No Open Question covers it (Q-01 concerns whether lower tiers deliver tagged files; Q-03 concerns AI stem separation).
findings.evidence: 14.05.04-tagged-preview-untagged-delivery.md:95 (D-03): "| D-03 | The platform recommends a minimum tag density rather than accepting any interval | Too-sparse tagging is theft the producer won't notice until the beat is on someone's record. |" · 14.05.04-tagged-preview-untagged-delivery.md:31-33 (Behavior): "Tag placement is the whole design: intervals must be frequent enough that removing them by editing destroys the beat, sparse enough that a buyer can hear the music. Get it wrong in either direction and the feature fails — silently, as either theft or lost sales." · 14.05.04-tagged-preview-untagged-delivery.md:41 (Happy Path 2): "System generates a tagged preview, overlaying the tag at the producer's chosen interval." · 14.05.04-tagged-preview-untagged-delivery.md:51 (Edge Cases): "| Tag placed too sparsely | The beat is editable — cut the tagged bars, loop the rest, and it's stolen | Producer's choice; the platform should recommend a minimum density, not just accept any value |" · 14.05.04-tagged-preview-untagged-delivery.md:68 (States): "| Empty | Producer hasn't set a tag | Publish gate — a beat cannot go public untagged; that's giving it away |" — the gate covers presence only.
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent (a) the numeric density floor — no value appears anywhere, in a domain that otherwise quantifies precisely (7-day cart hold, 72 h grant window, P95 < 300 ms audition) — and (b) whether falling below it blocks publish or merely displays advice. 'Frequent enough that removing them destroys the beat, sparse enough that a buyer can hear the music' is not testable as written.

findings.claim: 14.04.03 names an outcome in which a buyer's purchased project template becomes permanently unusable — the referenced sample pack was not bundled and has since been delisted — and gives it only a dead deferral target as its resolution. None of the file's three tracked questions reaches it: Q-01 is DAW session-format parsing, Q-02 is the legal question of whether a template *may* bundle third-party content, Q-03 is whether templates belong in domain 14 at all. D-02 (total completion cost shown before the buy button) addresses the pre-purchase disclosure but says nothing about a dependency that disappears after purchase.
findings.evidence: 14.04.03-project-template-catalog-dependency-manifest.md:55 (Edge Cases): "| Vendor doesn't bundle, buyer can't get the loops (pack delisted) | Session permanently uncompletable for that buyer | `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` |" · The full tracked question set at 14.04.03-project-template-catalog-dependency-manifest.md:100-102 covers only DAW-format parsing (Q-01), the legality of bundling (Q-02) and store-vs-education placement (Q-03). · 14.04.03-project-template-catalog-dependency-manifest.md:93 (D-02): "Total completion cost (template + missing dependencies) is shown before the buy button | A £15 template that needs £400 of plugins is a £415 purchase." — pre-purchase only. · Contrast the delisting guarantee the buyer would reasonably expect to inherit, 14.03.02-versioning-updates-legacy-archive.md:96 (D-01): "Every version a buyer was entitled to remains permanently fetchable" — which protects versions of things the buyer owns, not a third-party dependency they never bought.
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent whether the buyer of a now-uncompletable template is refunded, notified, offered a substitute, or left with a dead product — and whether delisting a pack that other listings depend on is blocked, warned on, or unrestricted.

findings.claim: The lease-wins-the-race case in 14.05.02 has a dead deferral target and is not covered by the resolved questions or by the domain CX. Domain CX-18 resolves only the opposite ordering (exclusive commits first — the pending lease is refused). Q-01 resolves that prior leases survive an exclusive sale. Together these mean a lease landing microseconds before the exclusive is grandfathered — but D-03 requires the live-lease count to be disclosed *before* the exclusive purchase, and that disclosed count is now stale by exactly the lease that just landed. Nothing states whether the exclusive buyer is re-shown the count, given a consent break, or bound to a disclosure that was true when rendered and false at commit.
findings.evidence: 14.05.02-exclusive-rights-purchase-auto-delist.md:51 (Edge Cases): "| Lease checkout completes microseconds before the exclusive | The exclusive is encumbered by a lease sold after the buyer decided to buy | `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` |" · 14.05.02-exclusive-rights-purchase-auto-delist.md:90 (D-03): "| D-03 | The live-lease count is disclosed before an exclusive purchase | Per CX-02 — \"exclusive\" that shares the beat with 40 live leases is a word the buyer understands differently from the seller. |" · digital-goods-marketplace-cx.md:359 (CX-18 q5) resolves only the reverse order: "A non-exclusive lease checkout racing an exclusive checkout — resolved at the same hard-lock as CX-15; if the exclusive commits first, the pending lease is refused, not grandfathered." · 14.05.02-exclusive-rights-purchase-auto-delist.md:96 (Q-01, resolved): "**RESOLVED — they survive; the buyer takes subject to them.**"
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent whether the exclusive checkout re-validates the disclosed lease count at commit and forces a consent break (the rule 14.01.01 D-04 applies to terms changes), proceeds silently on the stale count, or refuses the exclusive — on a transaction that D-01 requires to be atomic and that transfers a copyright.

findings.claim: 14.02.04 presupposes that a chargeback automatically triggers a blacklist, then leaves the card-theft-victim case — where the chargeback was fraud committed against the buyer — to a dead deferral target. Whether an automatic chargeback-driven blacklist exists at all is itself unstated: D-01 says blacklisting is platform-adjudicated on vendor request, which describes a different trigger entirely. None of Q-01 (confirm vendor-requested/platform-adjudicated), Q-02 (enforcement grace window) or Q-03 (leaked-serial detection) covers the chargeback trigger.
findings.evidence: 14.02.04-serial-blacklisting-anti-piracy.md:52 (Edge Cases): "| Chargeback triggers automatic blacklist, but the chargeback was fraud against the *buyer* | Victim of card theft is punished twice | `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` |" · 14.02.04-serial-blacklisting-anti-piracy.md:87 (D-01): "| D-01 | Blacklisting is platform-adjudicated; vendors request, they do not execute | Per DT-02. The multi-hyphenate structure means vendor and buyer are the same population — unilateral kill switches let users disable each other. |" · The full tracked question set at 14.02.04-serial-blacklisting-anti-piracy.md:95-97 reaches none of it. · The chargeback path is otherwise specified with care elsewhere — 14.02.01-licence-issuance-entitlement-record.md:200 (D-10): "A **chargeback is recorded as a distinct trigger from a refund**, everywhere" — which makes the silence on its blacklisting consequence conspicuous rather than merely absent.
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent whether a chargeback blacklists automatically, and if so what protects a buyer whose card was stolen — D-02 guarantees a reason, notification and appeal route, but not whether the entitlement is suspended before or after that appeal resolves.

findings.claim: 14.06.03's hardware-return unwind — the buyer returns dead gear whose bundled licences have already transferred, while the seller may already have deactivated their machines — has a dead deferral target and is described by the file's own CX as its core unresolved case. 14.06.03's three decisions cover pre-purchase disclosure and buyer eligibility only; the two tracked questions do not reach the unwind. 14.09.02 D-12 rules the adjacent case in the opposite direction (a transferred-out entitlement is not refundable), which makes the hardware-return path's silence load-bearing rather than incidental.
findings.evidence: 14.06.03-bundled-software-with-used-hardware.md:52 (Edge Cases): "| Hardware arrives dead; buyer returns it | Licence must claw back (14.09.03) — and the seller may have already deactivated their machines | `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` — CX-02's core unresolved case |" · 14.06.03-bundled-software-with-used-hardware.md:89-91 (D-01/D-02/D-03) cover only proactive surfacing of bundled licences, per-licence transfer-state display, and pre-purchase buyer eligibility. · 14.09.02-digital-refund-eligibility-adjudication.md:285 (D-12): "| D-12 | A transferred-out entitlement (14.06.02) is **not refundable**, and this is stated at the point of transfer | Per DT-11. The seller was made whole by the resale; the alternatives are punishing an innocent third-party buyer or paying twice for one licence. |" · 14.06.02-licence-transfer-escrow.md:96 (D-01) requires atomic settlement — "any failure rolls back entirely" — but the hardware return arrives long after settlement has succeeded.
findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent whether a hardware return reverses the licence transfer at all, who absorbs the loss when the seller has already deactivated and been paid, and how this reconciles with 14.09.02 D-12's rule that transferred-out entitlements are not refundable.
